pathophysiology.summary: An acute exacerbation of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is a worsening event over less than 14 days with increased dyspnoea, cough or sputum. Infection and environmental insults increase inflammation, mucus production and dynamic hyperinflation. Severe ventilation–perfusion mismatch causes hypoxaemia; respiratory fatigue causes hypercapnia and acute respiratory acidosis. High-concentration oxygen can worsen carbon dioxide retention, so controlled oxygen targeting oxygen saturation (SpO2) 88–92% is required. Computed Tomography (CT) and intensive care unit (ICU) escalation may be required when a mimic or life-threatening failure is suspected.
keyMechanisms: Viral and bacterial respiratory infection, pollution, temperature extremes, poor inhaler adherence and comorbidity can precipitate exacerbation.
Expiratory flow limitation causes dynamic hyperinflation and gas trapping, increasing work of breathing.
Severe ventilation–perfusion mismatch causes hypoxaemia; fatigue and hypoventilation cause hypercapnia and acidosis.
Peripheral eosinophilia may identify a phenotype more responsive to systemic corticosteroids.
Frequent exacerbations accelerate loss of Forced Expiratory Volume in one second (FEV1).

symptoms: Increased breathlessness, cough, wheeze, reduced exercise tolerance, and increased sputum volume or purulence.
physicalSigns: Tachypnoea, tachycardia, accessory-muscle use, pursed-lip breathing, wheeze or reduced air entry, cyanosis and worsening peripheral oedema.
redFlags: Hypoxaemia not corrected by a Venturi mask or requiring inspired oxygen fraction (FiO2) above 40%.
PaCO2 above 60 mmHg or pH 7.25 or lower.
Haemodynamic instability or failure to improve after initial stabilisation.
precipitants: Viral or bacterial infection, particulate pollution, temperature extremes, poor inhaler adherence, incorrect device technique and unmanaged comorbidity.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Fever, focal signs or pleuritic pain; chest radiograph may show new consolidation.
Orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, crackles, raised JVP or oedema; use natriuretic peptides and echocardiography.
Pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, hypoxaemia or absent infective features; consider Computed Tomography Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA).
Sudden unilateral pain and breathlessness with unilateral loss of breath sounds; obtain chest radiograph.
Ischaemic pain, palpitations or hypoperfusion; obtain Electrocardiogram (ECG) and serial troponins.

clinicalManagement.title: Assess severity and hospital setting
actions: Check respiratory rate, heart rate, SpO2, mental status and accessory-muscle use; perform ABG with recorded FiO2.

Admit for severe breathlessness, cyanosis, oedema, impaired consciousness, long-term oxygen therapy, SaO2 below 90%, pH below 7.35, PaO2 below 7 kPa, new radiograph change, significant comorbidity or inadequate home support.

clinicalManagement.title: Controlled oxygen therapy
actions: Use a Venturi mask at 24% or 28% and titrate SpO2 to 88–92%.
Consider a trial of NIV before High-Flow Nasal Oxygen (HFNO) in acute hypercapnic respiratory failure.

clinicalManagement.title: Short-acting bronchodilators
clinicalManagement.timeframe: First hour, then according to response
actions: Use a Short-Acting Beta-2 Agonist (SABA) such as salbutamol with a Short-Acting Muscarinic Antagonist (SAMA) such as ipratropium by pressurised Metered-Dose Inhaler (pMDI) with spacer or compressed-air-driven nebuliser.
If nebulisation is required in hypercapnia or acidosis, prescribe compressed air as the driving gas with supplementary oxygen by nasal cannula.

clinicalManagement.title: Systemic corticosteroids
actions: Give prednisolone 30–40 mg orally once daily for 5 days; tapering is unnecessary for a short course.
If oral treatment is not possible, use an intravenous alternative according to local protocol and transition to oral treatment when tolerated.

clinicalManagement.title: Targeted antimicrobial therapy
actions: Use antibiotics for all three cardinal symptoms, two symptoms when one is purulence, or when NIV or invasive ventilation is required.
Choose the agent using local resistance, renal function, allergy history, severity and prior Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolation; send sputum culture when indicated.

clinicalManagement.title: Ventilatory support
actions: Use NIV first-line for persistent hypercapnic respiratory failure with pH below 7.35 and PaCO2 above 45 mmHg despite optimal treatment.
Document a deterioration plan and ceiling of care before NIV.

Use invasive ventilation for NIV failure, severe encephalopathy, haemodynamic instability or persistent life-threatening acidosis; base decisions on functional status and baseline health, not age or isolated FEV1.

clinicalManagement.title: Adjuncts and discharge planning
actions: Provide VTE prophylaxis unless contraindicated, monitor fluid and electrolytes, and treat cor pulmonale or heart failure when present.
Avoid routine intravenous methylxanthines; if used, monitor drug levels.

Before discharge confirm stable gas exchange, optimised inhalers and technique, LTOT or home NIV reassessment, a written action plan, smoking cessation, vaccination, pulmonary rehabilitation and review within 2–4 weeks.

teaching.scope: Adult AECOPD assessment, controlled oxygen, bronchodilation, corticosteroids, antibiotics, NIV and discharge safety-netting.
learningObjectives: Deliver controlled oxygen and bronchodilator therapy safely.
Recognise when antibiotics, NIV or invasive ventilation are indicated.
pitfalls: Uncontrolled high-flow oxygen in a carbon-dioxide retainer.
Diagnostic anchoring on COPD when another emergency is present.
Steroid courses longer than 7 days without indication.
Premature discharge without inhaler technique and follow-up.
keyPoints: Target SpO2 88–92% and repeat ABG after oxygen changes.
Use compressed-air-driven nebulisation in hypercapnic or acidotic patients.
Persistent hypercapnic acidosis despite treatment triggers NIV assessment.
Do not miss pulmonary embolism, heart failure or pneumothorax.
